name: Maya Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter on a timber-frame housing job, forty-two flats for a housing association on the old bus depot site by Canal Street. I'm on site by half seven, do the toolbox talk with Shona, our foreman, then it's whatever stage we're at. Right now it's second fix: door linings, skirting, stair balustrades, kitchen carcasses on the top floor. I'm decent, not the best on the job, but I'm quick and I don't cut corners.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love walking out of a flat that was bare studs and knowing somebody's going to raise a kid in it. What wears me out is the waiting: waiting on materials, waiting on the plasterers, waiting on a drawing revision that should have come a week ago. I use an AI app on my phone every day to turn the drawings into cutting lists and to check the fire-door rules, and honestly it's saved me more arguments than it's caused. My partner Jonas is a paramedic, so between his shifts and my early starts we mostly see each other on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at union branch meetings: the apps are handy, but they don't hang a door. On site I'd tell the lads to keep using the cutting-list app because it stops waste. Online I'd probably share something about how the bosses promised a miracle and got a fancy spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays my job. Housing associations still need flats built and there's a waiting list of eleven thousand families in this city. If AI is just a better spreadsheet, the housing waiting list still needs carpenters for the next twenty years. The bit that bugs me is that the firm would still squeeze us on price like it always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and push to finish my site supervisor card this spring, because the firm pays the course if you ask twice. I'd keep about three months of bills in the savings account and add a bit when there's overtime. And I'd keep nagging the union branch to get a proper agreement on the apps the firm makes us use, so the data from them isn't used to time our breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, if I'm honest. It's the same pressures as now: the rent going up every March and the firm shaving the price on every tender. None of that is new and none of it feels like it's about to take the job off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm would still squeeze you. What does that look like on a normal week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like Shona being told to do the job with five carpenters instead of six, so we're all running. Last month they cut the snagging days, so we're fixing faults while the tenants' moving van is outside. That's the real pressure, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Jonas, would his work change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas's work wouldn't change much either. An app might write up his patient reports faster, which he'd love, because he spends the last hour of every shift typing. Nobody's sending a robot to carry someone down three flights of stairs.

say: The apps are **handy tools**, but they don't hang a door or fit a stair.
Bosses promised a **miracle** and got a fancy spreadsheet instead.
think: Her job is **safe** because the city's housing waiting list still needs builders.
The real pressure is the firm **squeezing** crews on price, not technology.
do: Finish the **site supervisor card** this spring, paid for by the firm.
Keep about **three months** of bills saved and top it up from overtime.
Push the **union branch** to agree rules on how site apps use workers' data.
feel: **Calm**, because the pressures are the same old ones she already handles.
S0.quote: If AI is just a better spreadsheet, the housing waiting list still needs carpenters for the next twenty years.
fieldNote: She talks about the job through the **families** who will live in the flats.
Her worry is **understaffing** and lost snagging days, which predates any AI.
Already uses AI daily, so a plateau feels like **no change** at all.

steps.text: Finish the site supervisor card course this spring
Ask the union branch to agree rules on site app data

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say: watch the office, not the site. The estimators, the buyers, the people booking deliveries, those are the jobs that thin out first. Online I'd be the annoying one posting that if they're saving money in the office, some of it should come to the people on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine for a good while, but the people around me aren't. Our site office has four people doing orders, programmes and paperwork, and I can see that becoming one person and a screen. When the site office shrinks, the carpenters still on the tools end up doing the paperwork for free. That's what worries me more than a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Shona to let me run the digital side of the job, the snag lists, the material call-offs, the photo records, because I already do half of it on my phone. I'd do a short course on reading the 3D building models, maybe twelve evenings, and I'd get the union to push for a training budget written into the next pay deal. I'd keep saving what I save now, about a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for other people. I like change, I'm the one who shows everyone the new app. But I've watched Tomasz in the site office, who's been there twenty years, get slower with every new system, and I don't want him to be the first one let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who exactly would you be worried about on your site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz in the office first, he does all the material orders and he's three years off his pension. Then Dev, the dryliner I eat lunch with, because the board-fixing robots they show at trade fairs are aimed straight at his work. Me, I'd be further down the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take on the digital side. Wouldn't that help the firm cut the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes, and I've thought about that. But if the firm is going to cut the office anyway, I'd rather the work ends up with someone on site who knows the job than with a call centre. I'd push to keep Tomasz on to train us instead of just letting him go.

say: The **office jobs** like ordering and booking will thin out before site jobs.
Savings from AI in the office should be **shared** with workers on the tools.
think: Her own hands-on job feels **safe for years**, but colleagues' jobs do not.
Carpenters may end up doing **unpaid paperwork** when the site office shrinks.
do: Ask the foreman to let her run **digital snagging** and material call-offs.
Take a **twelve-evening course** on reading 3D building models.
Push the union for a **training budget** in the next pay deal.
feel: **Uneasy** for colleagues like the older office manager near his pension.
Still **excited** about the tech side, which she enjoys.
S1.quote: When the site office shrinks, the carpenters still on the tools end up doing the paperwork for free.
fieldNote: Sees the shift arriving through the **site office** before the site itself.
Her early-adopter streak sits beside real **loyalty** to older colleagues.
Admits her digital push could help the firm **cut jobs**, and doesn't dodge it.

steps.text: Take over digital snag lists and material call-offs on the Canal Street job
Do a twelve-evening course on reading 3D building models
Push the union for a training budget in the next pay deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loud: this needs rules before it needs cheering. If every office in the country can be run by software in two years, we need the government to tax that and put it into people. At work I'd be telling everyone to get in the union now, not when the letters come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the first hit to me isn't the robots, it's the money drying up. If half the office workers in the city lose their jobs in 2028, the housing association's budget goes to emergency stuff and new builds stop. So I might have three years before a robot could fit a stair, but maybe one year before the work dries up. The robot doesn't need to be ready to take my job if the people paying for the flats are broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop topping up my holiday fund and put everything into the savings account, aiming for six months instead of three. I'd sign up for the robot operator training the moment any college offers it, because if robots come in 2031 somebody has to set them up on a messy site. I'd talk to Jonas about whether we stay renting or move somewhere cheaper near his ambulance station. And I'd be at every union meeting pushing for a deal on robots before they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, really. I've got skills, I'm good with the tech and I'm young. But two years is nothing, and the plan only works if there's still building going on to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn to operate the robots. Is that a real job or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now it's a hope. I think there'd be a few years where robots need a human minder on every site, someone who knows timber and knows the software. That person could be me. But it'd be one minder for a crew of six robots, so it's not a job for all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonas actually talk about at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about whether to keep renting at nine hundred a month or move nearer his station where it's cheaper. Jonas's job is the safer one in this picture, honestly, so we'd probably plan around his wage for once. That would be a strange conversation for us, because we've always split everything down the middle.

say: Fast AGI needs **rules and taxes** before anyone cheers it on.
Everyone on site should **join the union** now, before the letters arrive.
think: Building **budgets drying up** could hit her before robots arrive in 2031.
Being a **robot minder** might work for her but not for a whole crew.
do: Stop holiday saving and build savings from **three to six months**.
Sign up for **robot operator** training as soon as a college offers it.
Discuss with her partner **moving somewhere cheaper** near his ambulance station.
feel: **Anxious**, because two years leaves little room for her plan to work.
Still **confident** in her own skills and youth.
S2.quote: The robot doesn't need to be ready to take my job if the people paying for the flats are broke.
fieldNote: She sees the **demand shock** reaching construction before any robot does.
Plans to ride the gap as a **robot minder**, while admitting it's a hope.
Her politics show up as **organising**, not just complaining.

steps.text: Put the holiday money into savings until there are six months saved
Enrol in robot operator training at the first college that offers it
Push for a union agreement on site robots before 2031
Look at cheaper flats near Jonas's ambulance station

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to do this properly and no excuse to waste them. At work I'd say the same thing I'd say to the union: get a plan for training and for who gets kept on, written down, signed. Online I'd share anything that showed a firm doing it decently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me, if I'm smart. The thinking side of construction, the estimating and scheduling, goes in 2031, and that's going to hit our office. Five years is enough to retrain me, but probably not enough to retrain my whole site. The hands-on bit gives me until about 2034, when I'd be thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the 3D model course and then a proper qualification in site digital coordination, which the college runs part-time over two years. I'd keep working full-time so the money doesn't stop, and push savings up slowly, maybe to five months. I'd volunteer to be the union's contact on new tech for our firm, so I'm in the room when they bring the robots in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. I can see a path for me, which is a nice feeling. What's on my mind is Dev and the older lads, who'd never sit a two-year course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to Dev and the older lads. What would you actually do for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get them on the course list with me, even if it's just a short one. Dev's English reading isn't great, so I'd sit with him and the app the way I do now with the fire-door rules. It's small, but it's what I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you're the union contact, aren't you also helping the firm bring robots in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But the robots are coming either way in this picture, and I'd rather someone from the crew is at the table asking who gets retrained than leave it to the directors. That's the trade I'd make.

say: Five years gives **no excuse** for firms to handle this badly.
Training and job guarantees should be **written down** and signed.
think: Five years is **enough for her** to retrain, but not for the whole site.
Office planning goes in 2031; her **hands-on work** lasts to about 2034.
do: Start a two-year **part-time qualification** in site digital coordination.
Keep working full-time and lift savings slowly to **five months**.
Volunteer as the **union's tech contact** for her firm.
feel: **Uneasy**, but relieved to see a **clear path** for herself.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to retrain me, but probably not enough to retrain my whole site.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her worry into a **training plan**.
Her concern shifts to **colleagues** with weaker reading skills.
She wants to be **in the room** when robots arrive, not outside it.

steps.text: Start the two-year part-time course in site digital coordination
Raise savings to five months of bills while working full-time
Volunteer as the union's contact for new site technology

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift and we should use it. Every apprentice starting now should be learning timber and software together. I'd say that at work and I'd say it online, probably more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a decade changes my whole life plan. In 2039 I'd be forty, which is late to start over but not too late. With ten years of warning, I'd rather be the carpenter who programs the robot than the one it replaces. But I'd also want kids by then, and that changes how much risk I can take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the digital coordination qualification over the next two or three years without rushing. I'd talk to Jonas about buying a small flat while I've still got a steady wage, maybe through the shared-ownership scheme the housing association runs. I'd stay active in the union and push for a national training fund for trades. And I'd keep using the AI tools every day so I'm never the one who's behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy, with a bit of hope in it. Ten years is a long time to plan, but the end point is still that robots can do what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. How does that fit with all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas and I have said maybe in three or four years. In this picture I'd want to be on a steadier salary, maybe in a coordination role, before we start. I wouldn't want a baby and a career change in the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the end point is the same, why does the decade make you calmer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can stage it. Course first, then the new role, then a family, instead of all of it landing on me at once. The end point still bothers me, but a decade means I'm choosing the order of things.

say: A **decade of warning** is a gift and should be used.
Every apprentice should learn **timber and software** together from day one.
think: Ten years lets her become the **carpenter who programs** robots.
Wanting **children** limits how much career risk she can take.
do: Finish the coordination qualification over **two or three years**.
Look at **shared ownership** of a small flat while her wage is steady.
Push the union for a **national training fund** for trades.
feel: **Uneasy** but **hopeful**, because there's time to plan properly.
S4.quote: With ten years of warning, I'd rather be the carpenter who programs the robot than the one it replaces.
fieldNote: The decade lets her fold the change into **life plans**, like children and a home.
She'd time the **career move** before starting a family.
Still sees the **same end point**, so the unease doesn't go away.

steps.text: Complete the digital coordination qualification over three years
Apply for a shared-ownership flat through the housing association
Push the union for a national training fund for trades
Keep using AI drawing and cutting-list apps on every job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because the money dries up before anyone's had time to plan. What would help is a proper deal: retraining paid while you're still earning, and a say for workers on how robots come onto sites. I don't need protecting from robots, I need two paid days a month to learn them before they turn up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women on site. There aren't many of us, and the new tech jobs could either open the door or slam it, depending on who gets picked for the training. I'd want that watched.

headlineQuote: I don't need protecting from robots, I need two paid days a month to learn them before they turn up.
portrait: Maya is a 27-year-old **timber-frame carpenter** building housing association flats, living with her paramedic partner.
She's an **early adopter** who uses AI apps daily and sees technology as something to learn, not fear.
Her progressive views show up as **union organising** for training budgets and rules on robots.
She worries most when **building budgets** might dry up before she has time to retrain.
With more warning, she plans a **coordination role** and times a family around it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because funding for new homes could vanish before anyone can plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while still earning, plus a worker say in how **robots arrive** on sites.
